Figure 5: Examples of (a) space cooling only HP-TES chiller-ice storage system [35] and (b)space heating-based HP-TES system [14] To leverage HP-TES load-shifting capabilities in both cooling and heating modes, one option is to use two TES tanks, one hot and one cold, to reduce peak loads, as experimentally demonstrated by Moreno et al.[36]. In this study, a water-to-water HP was combined with two PCM-TES tanks for charging purposes: one connected to the evaporator (PCM temperature: 10°C) and the other to the condenser (PCM temperature: Page 10 of 127 DE-EE0009681 University of Maryland, College Park 46°C). Both tanks utilize salt-hydrate PCMs, which are macro-encapsulated in modules within a PCM heat-transfer fluid tank. In discharge mode, the tanks are directly connected to a prototype building through hydronic loops and three-way valves. Comparisons were made between the PCM tanks, and only sensible water storage was conducted, showing that the PCM tank can store 33.5% more energy per volume, maintaining indoor setpoint conditions by 21% longer. Nonetheless, the recharge time for the PCM tanks was 4.6 times higher. Challenges occurred in charging the TES due to PCM supercooling and the low PCM thermal conductivities. While the literature has shown the need to reduce peak demand as much as possible, it is important to investigate the conditions under which demand reduction can yield energy savings. To this end, Hirschey et al. [37] conducted an exploratory study on appropriate TES temperatures, employing a Carnot COP approach to assess both demand reduction and energy-saving potential. In line with the literature, lower TES temperatures in cooling mode provided greater cooling demand reduction, and vice versa in heating (i.e., higher TES temperatures yield greater heating demand reductions). However, this increases overall energy requirements, as more energy is needed to recharge the TES. Therefore, it is important to keep the TES temperature as close as possible to the application's temperature to achieve energy savings. This leads to the option of integrating a single TES which utilizes near-room-temperature PCMs (20–30°C) with HP systems to load-shift in both cooling and heating modes (Figure 6). These room-temperature PCM-TES minimize compressor power by reducing the temperature lifts, i.e., increasing heating-mode evaporating temperatures and reducing cooling-mode condensing temperatures [38]. A techno-economic study was conducted using simplified models and rule-based controls to assess the peak savings in different locations. Results indicate that higher peak reductions can be achieved in extreme climatic locations. Furthermore, PCMs around 20°C favored cooling-dominated regions, while PCMs around 30°C favored heating-dominated areas, consistent with the temperature-lift dependence.
